steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a database paper proposing a polystore/federated architecture that uses provenance and a knowledge graph to query data that is not explicitly connected across heterogeneous data stores. Use an Oil & Gas workflow scenario as motivation, state the research question, review existing solutions, and summarize the architecture, implementation, evaluation and paper structure.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Modern applications manipulate diverse, heterogeneous data
- Motivating scenario: Oil & Gas workflows feeding DL models
- The user's query problem and the research question
- Existing solutions and their limits; MDBS and polystores
- Our proposal: federated architecture with provenance-based linkage
- Implementation with a knowledge graph (Hyperknowledge)
- Evaluation against PostgreSQL FDW; paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Diverse datasets, different models/usages, specific tools: medical informatics, oceanography, metagenomics, exploration and production in Oil & Gas
- Scenario (Figure 1)
  - oil reserves discovery; independent workflows process large raw data files -> training/validation datasets for Deep Learning (DL) models
  - no direct relationships between workflows; activities consume/produce data in heterogeneous stores, data not directly linked
  - workflow 1: geological raw files -> metadata; missing/displaced info as metadata quality; files on Parallel File System, quality score + metadata in relational DBMS (R-DBMS)
  - workflow 2: high-quality files -> geospatial indexes to speed geospatial queries; stored in document-oriented DBMS (Doc DBMS)
  - workflow 3: augments raw geodata with knowledge from geoscience experts; Triplestore System (T-DBMS)

  - user: Machine Learning (ML) expert with deep domain knowledge; must query heterogeneous stores when reporting ML model
  - e.g., geographic coordinates from SEG-Y file used for training/validation files + spatial resolution between slices in seismic data -> file + document database
  - needs specific tools for both systems and knowledge of how data inter-relates (which file lines relate to which objects)
  - challenges: (i) access to heterogeneous stores; (ii) linkage of data in remote distinct stores
  - RQ: How to query data that are not explicitly connected residing on heterogeneous data stores?
- Existing solutions
  - distributed file systems (GFS, HDFS), NoSQL (MongoDB, AllegroGraph), frameworks (Spark), hybrid multimodal (OrientDB), hybrid NewSQL (LeanXcale)
  - each handles few data models/formats; doesn't address diverse datasets
  - migrating to single database/schema doesn't work: costly, time-consuming conversion/loading; integration of disparate data (structured with text, web pages, semi-structured, time series)
  - no DBMS performs well on all data: one size does not fit all
  - need middleware with seamless interface, independent data model and (perhaps) schemes
  - MDBS (federated data system): layer on top of autonomous data systems sharing portions of data; integrated access
  - polystore: kind of MDBS; integrated access to NoSQL, RDBMS, HDFS, sometimes through processing framework
  - still lacking abstraction and query language
- Our proposal
  - federated architecture encapsulating heterogeneous sources + provenance for data linkage (explicit links from provenance of workflow activity execution)
  - provenance: process and data used to derive data product; causality = dependency relationships (data-process, data dependencies)
  - abstract layer: queries on global conceptual schema; data mappings and record linkage transparent to consumers
  - features (i)-(vii): global conceptual schema; local conceptual schemas; mappings; workflows' provenance schema; instrumentation of applications; provenance capture; query processing

  - models for schemas, mappings, provenance schema and execution; stored in Knowledge Graph using Hyperknowledge (HK), hybrid conceptual model for media content and meaning
  - HK context element to encapsulate and modularize models and data

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Several modern applications manipulate diverse datasets that have different models and usages, and they employ specific tools and techniques, e.g., applications in medical informatics, oceanography, metagenomics, and the exploration and production phases in Oil & Gas.

For example, in an oil reserves discovery scenario, independent workflows process big raw data files to generate training and validation datasets that are used by Deep Learning (DL) models, as shown in Figure 1. The workflows do not have direct relationships, but they have several activities that consume and generate data from/to heterogeneous data stores where the data are not directly linked.

The first workflow processes geological raw data files to extract the necessary metadata. It also assesses missing and displaced information, as a measurement of metadata quality. The data files are on a Parallel File System, while the data quality score and the extracted metadata are stored in a relational DBMS (R-DBMS). The second workflow takes the high-quality data files and generates geospatial indexes. This data is used to speed up geospatial queries over the geological data and it is stored in a document-oriented DBMS (Doc DBMS). The third workflow also takes the high-quality data files and it augments the raw geodata files with extra knowledge given by geoscience experts. This meta-information is stored in a Triplestore System (T-DBMS). Finally, the last workflow prepares the learning datasets used by DL algorithms. It queries the data from the Doc DBMS and the related knowledge from the T-DBMS to generate the datasets, which are stored as HDF5 files in the Parallel File System, so they are ready to be used by DL algorithms.

In this scenario, the user is a Machine Learning (ML) expert who has deep knowledge in the domain. When he/she reports the ML model, he/she has to query the data that is in the heterogeneous data stores. For instance, he/she should run a query to find out what are the geographic coordinates extracted from the SEG-Y file that is used to produce the training and validation files and the spatial resolution between slices in the seismic data. To answer this query, he/she has to inspect data in the file and in the document database. Besides using specific tools to access both systems, the user also has to know how the data is inter-related, i.e., which lines of the file are related to which objects of the document database. These issues show the challenges of these scenarios: (i) the access to heterogeneous data stores; (ii) the linkage of heterogeneous data that is in remote distinct data stores.

The research question of our work can be shortly stated as How to query data that are not explicitly connected residing on heterogeneous data stores?

- Existing solutions: distributed file systems (GFS, HDFS), NoSQL (MongoDB, AllegroGraph), Spark, OrientDB, LeanXcale; each covers few models/formats
  - migrating to one database/schema: costly conversion, disparate data; one size does not fit all
  - need middleware; MDBS (federated) layer on autonomous stores; polystore as a kind of MDBS; still lacking abstraction and query language
- Proposal: federated architecture + provenance (causality) for data linkage; global conceptual schema; features (i)-(vii)
- Implementation: RESTful microservice; Knowledge Graph with Hyperknowledge (HK); HK context element
- Evaluation: Oil & Gas scenario; vs PostgreSQL FDW; more than two times less complex queries; overhead not greater than 30%
- Organization: Sections 2-6

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Several modern applications manipulate diverse datasets that have different models and usages, and they employ specific tools and techniques, e.g., applications in medical informatics, oceanography, metagenomics, and the exploration and production phases in Oil & Gas.

For example, in an oil reserves discovery scenario, independent workflows process big raw data files to generate training and validation datasets that are used by Deep Learning (DL) models, as shown in Figure 1. The workflows do not have direct relationships, but they have several activities that consume and generate data from/to heterogeneous data stores where the data are not directly linked.

The first workflow processes geological raw data files to extract the necessary metadata. It also assesses missing and displaced information, as a measurement of metadata quality. The data files are on a Parallel File System, while the data quality score and the extracted metadata are stored in a relational DBMS (R-DBMS). The second workflow takes the high-quality data files and generates geospatial indexes. This data is used to speed up geospatial queries over the geological data and it is stored in a document-oriented DBMS (Doc DBMS). The third workflow also takes the high-quality data files and it augments the raw geodata files with extra knowledge given by geoscience experts. This meta-information is stored in a Triplestore System (T-DBMS). Finally, the last workflow prepares the learning datasets used by DL algorithms. It queries the data from the Doc DBMS and the related knowledge from the T-DBMS to generate the datasets, which are stored as HDF5 files in the Parallel File System, so they are ready to be used by DL algorithms.

In this scenario, the user is a Machine Learning (ML) expert who has deep knowledge in the domain. When he/she reports the ML model, he/she has to query the data that is in the heterogeneous data stores. For instance, he/she should run a query to find out what are the geographic coordinates extracted from the SEG-Y file that is used to produce the training and validation files and the spatial resolution between slices in the seismic data. To answer this query, he/she has to inspect data in the file and in the document database. Besides using specific tools to access both systems, the user also has to know how the data is inter-related, i.e., which lines of the file are related to which objects of the document database. These issues show the challenges of these scenarios: (i) the access to heterogeneous data stores; (ii) the linkage of heterogeneous data that is in remote distinct data stores.

The research question of our work can be shortly stated as How to query data that are not explicitly connected residing on heterogeneous data stores?

Several data management solutions have appeared to handle heterogeneous data access, like distributed file systems (e.g., GFS and HDFS), NoSQL databases (e.g., MongoDB, AllegroGraph), new data processing frameworks (e.g., Spark), and hybrid multimodal (e.g., OrientDB) or hybrid NewSQL (e.g., LeanXcale). In general, each solution handles a few kinds of data models or formats and it does not address the diverse datasets that modern applications need. On the other hand, migrating the heterogeneous data to a single database and schema does not work. Data conversion and loading is a very costly and time-consuming task, which is hard to justify, and it may involve integrating disparate data (e.g., integration of structured data with text, web pages, semi-structured data, time series). Also, no DBMS has high performance in all kinds of data, i.e., one size does not fit all.

So a middleware that gives a seamless interface with an independent data model and (perhaps) data schemes is needed to access heterogeneous data stores. A Multidatabase System (MDBS) (or federated data system) gives a software layer that runs on top of individual autonomous data systems (or data stores) that share portions of their data. The MDBS lets users access the various databases in an integrated way. A polystore system, which is a kind of MDBS, gives integrated access to several data stores, like NoSQL, RDBMS, or HDFS, sometimes through a data processing framework. But there is still a lack of abstraction and query language for accessing heterogeneous data stores in an integrated way.

To answer our research question, we propose a federated data system architecture that encapsulates heterogeneous data sources and also uses provenance for data linkage, i.e., we create the explicit links by collecting the provenance of the execution of the workflow activities. Provenance has information about the process and the data used to derive the data product. As the kind of provenance information we use causality, which is the dependency relationships among data products and the processes that generate them, like data-process dependencies and data dependencies. So the architecture gives users an abstract layer to formulate queries based on a global conceptual schema, and to process the user query it supports creating data mappings and record linkage that are transparent to service consumers. Its features are: (i) Creation of global conceptual schema (the domain schema); (ii) Creation of local conceptual schemas for each external heterogeneous data store; (iii) Creation of mappings between global and local conceptual schemas; (iv) Creation of workflows' provenance schema; (v) Instrumentation of the applications that run the workflows; (vi) Capture of provenance during workflows execution; (vii) Processing of user queries.

We show the proposed architecture by implementing it as a RESTful web service in a microservice architecture. We create models to represent the global conceptual schema, the local conceptual schemas, and the mappings among them, and also the provenance schema and execution. This information is stored in a Knowledge Graph made with Hyperknowledge (HK), which is a hybrid conceptual model that can handle the multitude of media content and the meaning behind this data. In particular, we use the context element of HK to encapsulate and modularize the models and the ingested data.

We evaluate the implementation of the architecture in a scenario that simulates a real case in the Oil & Gas industry, the one described earlier in this section. The evaluation looked at query complexity from the user perspective and from the system perspective. For the user we analyzed the query components (like keywords, involved entities), and for the system we analyzed query execution time. We compared the architecture against PostgreSQL FDW (Foreign Data Wrapper). PostgreSQL is a widely used commercial open-source database management system and FDW is a module that allows access to external data stores using SQL language and wrappers. Our results showed that the query is more than two times less complex than the same query written in SQL, and the overhead in query processing time is not greater than 30%. This indicates the applicability and utility of the architecture, although query processing time still needs more investigation and improvements.

The rest of this work is divided as follows. Section 2 presents the background and justifies our choices. Section 3 presents the proposed architecture. Section 4 presents the implementation of the proposal and its evaluation. Section 5 presents the related work. Section 6 presents the conclusion and proposals of future work.

On the other hand, migrating the heterogeneous data to a single database and schema does not work. Data conversion and loading is a very costly and time-consuming task that is difficult to justify, and it may involve the integration of disparate data (e.g., integration of structured data with text, web pages, semi-structured data, time series). Besides, no DBMS offers high performance for all kinds of data, i.e., one size does not fit all [4].

Therefore, a middleware that provides a seamless interface with an independent data model and (perhaps) data schemes is required to access heterogeneous data stores [4]. A Multidatabase System (MDBS) (or federated data system) provides a software layer that runs on top of individual autonomous data systems (or data stores) that share portions of their data, allowing users to access the various databases in an integrated way. A polystore system, a kind of MDBS, provides integrated access to several data stores, such as NoSQL, RDBMS, or HDFS, sometimes through a data processing framework [5]. Nevertheless, there is still a lack of abstraction and of a query language to access heterogeneous data stores in an integrated way [4].

To answer our research question, we propose a federated data system architecture that not only encapsulates heterogeneous data sources but also uses provenance for data linkage, i.e., we create the explicit links by collecting the provenance of the workflow activities' execution. Provenance contains information about the process and data used to derive the data product. We use causality as the kind of provenance information, i.e., the dependency relationships among data products and the processes that generate them, such as data-process dependencies and data dependencies [6]. The architecture thus provides users an abstract layer to formulate queries based on a global conceptual schema, and, to process the user query, it supports the creation of data mappings and record linkage transparent to service consumers. Its features are: (i) Creation of global conceptual schema (the domain schema); (ii) Creation of local conceptual schemas for each external heterogeneous data store; (iii) Creation of mappings between global and local conceptual schemas; (iv) Creation of workflows' provenance schema; (v) Instrumentation of the applications that run the workflows; (vi) Capture of provenance during workflows execution; (vii) Processing of user queries.

We demonstrate the proposed architecture through its implementation as a RESTful web service in a microservice architecture [7]. We devise models to represent the global conceptual schema, the local conceptual schemas, and the mappings among them, as well as the provenance schema and execution. This information is stored in a Knowledge Graph created using Hyperknowledge (HK), a hybrid conceptual model able to handle the multitude of media content and the meaning behind this data [8]. In particular, we use the context element of HK to encapsulate and modularize the models and ingested data.

We evaluate the architecture implementation in a scenario that simulates the real Oil & Gas case described earlier in this section. The evaluation considered query complexity from the user and system perspectives: for the former, we analyzed the query components (like keywords and involved entities), and for the latter, query execution time. We compared the architecture against PostgreSQL FDW (Foreign Data Wrapper). PostgreSQL is a widely used commercial open-source database management system, and FDW is a module that allows access to external data stores using SQL language and wrappers. Our evaluation results demonstrated that while the query is more than two times less complex than the same query written in SQL, the overhead in query processing time is not greater than 30%. This indicates the applicability and utility of the architecture, although further investigations and improvements are required in query processing time.

Section 4 presents the implementation of the proposal and its evaluation. Section 5 presents the related work. Section 6 presents the conclusion and proposals for future work.
